note: Scenarios written for this app (AI-drafted; a person must check them before release). The ideas come from The Art of Thinking Clearly, Thinking, Fast and Slow, The Great Mental Models and Super Thinking; no text is copied.

concepts.name: Sunk cost fallacy
concepts.idea: Carrying on with something because of what you've already put in, not because of what lies ahead.

concepts.name: Anchoring
concepts.idea: Letting the first number you hear pull your estimate towards it.

concepts.name: Confirmation bias
concepts.idea: Noticing what fits what you already believe, and skipping what doesn't.

concepts.name: Availability bias
concepts.idea: Judging how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind.

concepts.name: Survivorship bias
concepts.idea: Looking only at the winners that are left, and forgetting the ones that didn't make it.

concepts.name: Gambler's fallacy
concepts.idea: Thinking a random event is "due" because it hasn't happened for a while.

concepts.name: Hindsight bias
concepts.idea: Feeling, after something happens, that you knew it all along.

concepts.name: Bandwagon effect
concepts.idea: Doing or believing something because lots of other people do.

concepts.name: Overconfidence
concepts.idea: Being surer of what you know than your results show.

concepts.name: Framing effect
concepts.idea: Choosing differently when the same facts are put another way.

concepts.name: Halo effect
concepts.idea: Letting one good (or bad) trait colour how you judge everything else.

concepts.name: Base-rate neglect
concepts.idea: Ignoring how common something is in general when judging one case.

concepts.name: Authority bias
concepts.idea: Believing someone just because they seem important, even outside what they know.

concepts.name: Planning fallacy
concepts.idea: Thinking a task will take less time than it will, even when similar tasks took longer before.

concepts.name: Loss aversion
concepts.idea: Feeling a loss more strongly than a gain of the same size.

concepts.name: Mixing up correlation and cause
concepts.idea: Thinking that because two things happen together, one must cause the other.

concepts.name: Second-order thinking
concepts.idea: Asking "and then what?" to see what happens after the first effect.

concepts.name: Inversion
concepts.idea: Asking what would make things fail, then avoiding that.

concepts.name: First principles
concepts.idea: Breaking a problem down to the basic facts, then building a solution up from them.

concepts.name: Opportunity cost
concepts.idea: The real cost of a choice is the best thing you give up to make it.

concepts.name: Occam's razor
concepts.idea: When several explanations fit, start with the simplest one.

concepts.name: Hanlon's razor
concepts.idea: Don't assume someone meant harm when a mistake or forgetting explains it.

concepts.name: Circle of competence
concepts.idea: Knowing where your knowledge is strong, and being careful outside it.

concepts.name: The map is not the territory
concepts.idea: A model or summary is useful, but it leaves things out, and the real thing can differ.

concepts.name: The 80/20 rule
concepts.idea: Often a small part of the causes brings most of the results.

concepts.name: Compounding
concepts.idea: Small gains that build on each other grow much bigger over time.

concepts.name: Margin of safety
concepts.idea: Leave room for error, because things rarely go exactly to plan.

concepts.name: Thinking in chances
concepts.idea: Thinking about how likely each outcome is, instead of just yes or no.

items.text: Maya paid for a year of guitar lessons. After two months she hates them and would rather join the swim team, but she keeps going because "otherwise the money is wasted."
items.why: The money is spent either way. The only real question is which choice makes the rest of her year better.

items.text: Leo has queued for 40 minutes for a ride. A sign says the wait is another hour. He stays, saying he can't leave now after waiting so long.
items.why: The 40 minutes are gone whatever he does. He should only weigh the next hour against what else he could do with it.

items.text: A shop marks a jacket "Was 200, now 90!" Sam had planned to spend about 50 on a jacket, but 90 now feels like a bargain.
items.why: The 200 is an anchor. It makes 90 feel cheap, even though it's almost twice what Sam meant to spend.

items.text: One class is asked "Is the Nile longer or shorter than 20,000 km?" and another "…than 2,000 km?" When both then guess its length, the first class guesses much higher.
items.why: The number in the question pulls the guesses towards it, even though it was only a starting point.

items.text: Ava is sure her lucky socks help her team win. She remembers every win in them, but not the losses she also had in them.
items.why: She only counts the cases that agree with her belief. A fair test would count the losses too.

items.text: Noah thinks a new phone brand is bad, so he only reads the one-star reviews, and decides he was right.
items.why: Picking only the reviews that agree with you can make any brand look bad, or good.

items.text: After seeing news about a shark attack, Zoe is scared to swim in the sea, but she happily cycles in busy traffic every day.
items.why: Shark attacks are vivid and in the news, so they feel likely. Road accidents are far more common but rarely make headlines.

items.text: Raj thinks more English words start with K than have K as their third letter, because words like "kite" and "king" come to mind quickly.
items.why: It's easier to think of words by their first letter. In fact, more words have K third, like "ask" and "like".

items.text: "Old buildings were built better than new ones," says Ben, pointing at the beautiful 200-year-old houses in his town.
items.why: Plenty of old buildings were badly built too, but they fell down or were knocked down long ago. Only the best are left to see.

items.text: A video shows three famous people who dropped out of school and became rich. Kai decides school doesn't matter for success.
items.why: We hear about the few dropouts who became famous, not the many who struggled. The ones who didn't make it aren't in the video.

items.text: A coin lands heads five times in a row. Mia bets on tails, sure that tails is due now.
items.why: A fair coin has no memory. The next toss is still 50/50, whatever came before.

items.text: In a board game, Omar hasn't rolled a six for twenty turns. He's sure a six is more likely on his next roll.
items.why: Each roll of a fair die is separate. A six is still 1 in 6, however long it's been.

items.text: After the match, Lily says "I knew they would lose, it was obvious." Before it, she had said the game could go either way.
items.why: Once we know the result, it feels like it was predictable. Her own words before the match show it wasn't.

items.text: After a new game flops, Dan says the reasons were obvious and the makers should have seen it coming. He had pre-ordered it himself.
items.why: Knowing how it ended makes the warning signs look clear. At the time, Dan expected it to do well.

items.text: Two cafés stand side by side. One has a long queue and the other is empty, so Ella joins the queue, guessing that the busy one must be better.
items.why: A queue can start by chance and then grow because people copy each other. It's a hint, not proof of quality.

items.text: A new app goes viral and everyone in Finn's class downloads it, so he does too, without checking what it does with his data.
items.why: Lots of people using something doesn't make it right for you. It's still worth checking for yourself.

items.text: Before a test, Aria says she's 100% sure she'll get everything right without revising. She gets 60%.
items.why: Feeling sure isn't the same as knowing. Practice questions show how much you really know.

items.text: In surveys, most drivers say they are better than the average driver.
items.why: Not everyone can be above average. People tend to rate their own skills too highly.

items.text: Jay picks a yoghurt labelled "90% fat-free" over one labelled "contains 10% fat". Both have the same amount of fat.
items.why: Both labels say the same thing. Only the wording changed, but it changed his choice.

items.text: A doctor tells Grace an operation has a 90% survival rate, and she agrees to it. Her friend is told it has a 10% death rate, and refuses.
items.why: 90% surviving and 10% dying are the same fact. Putting it as a gain or a loss changes how it feels.

items.text: Ruby thinks the best footballer in her class must also give the best advice about homework.
items.why: Being good at one thing says little about another. One shining trait makes everything else look better too.

items.text: A video is beautifully filmed, with great music, so Max believes every fact in it without checking.
items.why: Good filming says nothing about whether the facts are true. The polish makes it seem more trustworthy than it is.

items.text: A quiet student who loves books: is he more likely studying to be a librarian or an engineer? Most people say librarian.
items.why: There are far more engineering students than library students, so even a quiet book lover is more likely to be one of them.

items.text: A test for a rare illness is 90% accurate. Joe tests positive and decides he almost certainly has it.
items.why: When an illness is rare, many positives are false alarms from all the healthy people tested. How common it is matters as much as how good the test is.

items.text: A famous actor in an advert says a vitamin boosts your brain, so Nia buys a year's supply.
items.why: Being a famous actor doesn't make someone an expert on vitamins. A claim like that needs evidence, not a celebrity.

items.text: In a game, the team captain states a rule that's clearly wrong, and nobody questions it because he's the captain.
items.why: Being in charge doesn't make someone right. It's fine to check a rule, whoever said it.

items.text: Ollie says his project will take one evening. His last three projects each took a whole weekend.
items.why: He's picturing the best case and ignoring how long the same kind of work took before. Past projects are the better guide.

items.text: A group plans to film a 3-minute video in an hour, forgetting the time needed to set up, re-film mistakes and edit.
items.why: Plans tend to skip the extra steps and the things that go wrong. Adding time for them makes a better plan.

items.text: Eva refuses a game where a coin toss wins her 15 points on heads and loses her 10 on tails, even though she'd expect to come out ahead.
items.why: On average she'd gain. But losing 10 feels worse than winning 15 feels good, so she says no.

items.text: Liam is upset all day about losing a 5-coin bet, but he barely noticed when he won 5 coins the day before.
items.why: The same amount felt much bigger as a loss than as a win.

items.text: In summer, ice-cream sales and sunburn both go up. Ali decides that eating ice cream causes sunburn.
items.why: Both rise because of a third thing: hot, sunny weather. Happening together doesn't mean one causes the other.

items.text: Students who eat breakfast get better grades, so a poster says breakfast makes you smarter.
items.why: Families with regular breakfasts may also have more sleep, routine and support. Other things could explain the link.

items.text: A town makes parking free to help its shops. Soon people who work in town fill every space all day, and shoppers can't find anywhere to park.
items.why: The first effect (cheaper parking) looked good. One more step of thinking would have shown who would really use the spaces.

items.text: Before spending all his game coins on a shortcut, Ari asks himself what he'll need them for next week.
items.why: He's thinking past the first result (a quick win) to what happens next (being short later).

items.text: Before a group project, Hana lists everything that could make it go badly (no plan, leaving it late, unclear jobs) and fixes each one first.
items.why: Instead of only asking how to succeed, she asked how it could fail and avoided that.

items.text: To keep his room tidy, Tariq asks "What makes it messy?" and puts a basket right where his clothes always pile up.
items.why: Turning the question around (what causes the mess?) shows the simplest fix.

items.text: Instead of copying other people's paper planes, Lena tests what makes a plane fly far (weight, wing size, folds) and designs her own.
items.why: She went back to the basic facts of flight and built up from them, rather than copying.

items.text: A bike shop wants 80 for a repair. Jon checks what's really broken, one cable and a brake pad worth about 12, and learns to fit them himself.
items.why: Breaking the problem down to its basic parts showed what it really takes.

items.text: Free tickets to a concert on the night before an exam aren't really free for Mila: she'd lose her last evening of revision.
items.why: The cost of a choice includes what you can't do instead. Here, that's revision time.

items.text: Rohan can spend Saturday earning 30 at a job or go to a free football camp. Choosing the camp costs him the 30 he could have earned.
items.why: Even a free choice costs the best thing you give up for it.

items.text: Ellie's phone won't turn on. Before deciding it's broken, she checks the simplest cause first: the battery is flat.
items.why: The simplest explanation that fits the facts is usually the best place to start.

items.text: The lights in a classroom flicker. Some students say it's a ghost; the teacher checks for a loose bulb first.
items.why: Prefer the explanation that needs the fewest extra assumptions.

items.text: Leah's friend hasn't replied to her message all day. Instead of deciding the friend is angry, Leah guesses she's busy or forgot.
items.why: A busy day or a slip is a more likely explanation than bad intentions.

items.text: A classmate bumps into Sam and spills his drink. Sam's first thought is "accident", not "he did it on purpose".
items.why: Most moments like this are accidents. Assuming bad intent starts needless fights.

items.text: Nora is great with computers and fixes her family's laptop, but she asks a mechanic about the strange noise the car is making.
items.why: She acts with confidence inside what she knows, and gets help outside it.

items.text: Asked about a subject he has never studied, Ivan says "I don't know enough to say" instead of guessing loudly.
items.why: Knowing where your knowledge ends is part of thinking well.

items.text: The map app shows a path through the park, but when Ola gets there it's closed for repairs.
items.why: A map is a simplified picture of the real place, and the real place can change or differ.

items.text: A game has an average rating of 4.5 stars, but the reviews say it crashes on the kind of phone Kim has.
items.why: One number sums up a lot, but it hides details that may matter to you.

items.text: Jade notices that most of her maths mistakes come from just two kinds of question, so she practises those first.
items.why: A few causes often explain most of a problem. Fixing them first brings the biggest gain.

items.text: A shop finds that a small share of its products brings in most of its sales, so it makes sure those are always in stock.
items.why: Results are often uneven: a few things matter far more than the rest.

items.text: Ben practises his tables for 5 minutes a day. Each day builds on the last, and after a few months he's much faster than friends who crammed once.
items.why: Small, regular gains add up and build on each other over time.

items.text: Money that earns interest also earns interest on its interest, so it grows a little faster every year.
items.why: Growth on top of growth speeds up over time.

items.text: The bus usually takes 20 minutes, but Iris leaves 35 minutes before her exam in case of traffic.
items.why: Planning in extra room means one delay doesn't ruin the day.

items.text: A bridge meant for 10-tonne trucks is designed to hold 30 tonnes.
items.why: Engineers build in extra strength because loads and materials are never exactly as expected.

items.text: Instead of saying "we'll definitely win", the coach says "we've got about a 60% chance, so let's prepare for both results".
items.why: Putting a rough chance on each outcome helps you prepare for more than one possibility.

items.text: A 70% chance of rain means Theo takes an umbrella, even though it might stay dry.
items.why: Acting on likelihoods rather than certainties leads to better choices on average.
